newsitem.title: UK: Irish premier was libelled, but gets no damages.
newsitem.headline: Irish premier was libelled, but gets no damages.

text.p: Former Irish prime minister Albert Reynolds was libelled by the Sunday Times, a London High Court jury decided on Tuesday.
But in a surprise ruling, the jury said the 64-year-old politician was not entitled to any damages.
The 24-day case focused on an allegation in the Sunday Times that Reynolds had misled the Dail (Irish parliament) and lied to his cabinet colleagues.
Reynolds had sued over a November 1994 story, which he branded a "horrible, vicious, vilifying article which it was unnecessary to write".

It said he did not give the full facts when he defended Harry Whelehan -- then recently promoted from Attorney-General to President of the High Court -- against criticism for delays in extraditing a paedophile priest, Brendan Smyth.
Whelehan's explanation that he had not seen the file or been told about it, and that it was a complex issue with no precedent, was all he knew when he first addressed the Dail, Reynolds said.
Reynolds denied deceiving his Labour coalition partner, Dick Spring, and some of his colleagues about what he knew.
The newspaper denied libel, pleading qualified privilege and justification.
It argued that Reynolds knew enough, the day before he spoke to the Dail, to form the view that Whelehan should not be sworn in as President of the High Court.

The foreman of the jury -- down to 11 since one of their number was taken ill early in the hearing -- told a packed courtroom that they had decided by a 10-1 majority that the allegation complained of by Reynolds was not "in substance true".
But he said the jury decided, also by a majority of 10-1, that neither journalist Alan Ruddock nor Sunday Times editor John Witherow had acted maliciously in publishing the piece.
